title: Flip-rate and Fidelity Playbook: Quantization Sanity Checks
content:
Purpose:
This note captures an operational playbook and a compact set of sanity-check experiments we ran to profile quantization-induced answer flips across micro-slices used during model onboarding. Goal is pragmatic: identify high-signal slices where AWQ vs GPTQ vs int8 produce reproducible fidelity deltas, recommend fast mitigations, and propose guardrails for model rollout decisions.

Background and motivation:
- Onboarding teams often need a small, high-payoff signal set to decide whether a quantized artifact is acceptable for production. Full slice sweeps are expensive and slow.
- We define flip-rate as the percent of prompts in a slice where the best-response category (pass/fail/factuality tier) changes after quantization. Flip-rate is complementary to aggregate metric deltas (EM/ROUGE/MAE) and often correlates more with user-visible regressions.
- This playbook documents our 10-slice quick-scan, metric definitions, observed failure modes, and recommended mitigations.

Experimental matrix (quick-scan):
- Models: base-llama-13b-v2 (fp16 baseline), awq-int4, gptq-int4, int8-ptq
- Slices (10 micro-cohorts): legal-instructions, math-short, math-long, factual-lookup, multi-step-reason, conversational-probing, code-generation-snippets, synthesis-multihop, multilingual-fragile, toxic-instruction-guardrails
- Per-slice sample size: 250 prompts (random stratified by difficulty where applicable)
- Metrics computed per slice: flip-rate, median-response-length, token-level-hallucination-rate (manual spot-check), exact-match (where defined), factuality-score (0-1 rubric), per-token-latency-ms (p90), cache-adjusted-cost-delta (%)
- Infrastructure: dedicated test pool on 1xA10 for fp16 baseline, A10 for quant variants; identical decoding params (temp=0.0 for factual slices, 0.7 for conversational slice).

Metric definitions (brief):
- Flip-rate: fraction of prompts where category changed (pass->fail, fail->pass, or factuality tier crosses threshold).
- Factuality-score: human-annotated 0/0.5/1 rubric, averaged per-slice (spot check n=40).
- Token-level-hallucination-rate: proportion of tokens in answers flagged as hallucinated in manual adjudication (n=40).
- Cache-adjusted-cost-delta: estimated percent change in per-request compute given measured latency and observed batching behavior.

Key findings (summary):
1) High flip-rate slices: factual-lookup and math-long showed the largest fidelity deltas for AWQ-int4 (flip-rate 12.4% and 9.6% respectively) vs baseline. GPTQ-int4 had lower flip-rates on factual-lookup (6.3%) but similar on math-long (8.9%).
2) Token-level hallucination increased most in conversational-probing under AWQ-int4 (from 2.1%->3.8% tokens flagged).
3) Code-generation-snippets: GPTQ-int4 produced more indentation/formatting errors (flip-rate 7.2%) but fewer factual function-name hallucinations than AWQ.
4) Multilingual-fragile slice displayed asymmetric regressions: AWQ degraded low-resource prompts (flip-rate 11%) while GPTQ stayed within noise (2.5%).
5) Latency and cost: int8-ptq reduced p90 per-token latency by ~18% and produced a 12% cache-adjusted cost reduction vs fp16; AWQ/GPTQ int4 showed variable CPU decode overheads that partially offset token speedups on the test harness.

Per-slice vignettes (selected):
- factual-lookup (n=250):
  * AWQ-int4: flip-rate 12.4% (31/250). Typical failure: short, high-precision numeric answers turned into rounded or omitted digits (e.g., '0.125' -> '0.12' or '0.13'), and occasional drop of citation sentences.
  * GPTQ-int4: flip-rate 6.3% (16/250). Failures skewed to long-context prompts where KV-cache alignment was suboptimal.
  * Note: human factuality-score delta AWQ -0.11, GPTQ -0.05 (on spot-check n=40).

- math-long (n=250):
  * Both AWQ and GPTQ show increased intermediate-step truncation errors; AWQ shows slightly more symbolic algebra mis-simplifications. Flip-rate AWQ 9.6% vs GPTQ 8.9%.
  * Hypothesis: reduced numeric stability in attention softmax and fused kernel precision.

- multilingual-fragile (n=250):
  * AWQ-int4 flip-rate 11% concentrated on Nepali and Tagalog prompts with mix-script. GPTQ-int4 flip-rate 2.5%.
  * Action: surface language-specific quantization calibration when language tags are present.

Failure-mode taxonomy (observed):
- Rounding/precision loss (numerical answers)
- KV-cache misalignment (long context)
- Tokenization boundary sensitivity (multilingual/morphologically rich languages)
- Decoder bit-noise amplified search heuristics (beam/topk instability)
- Surface-level formatting differences that break downstream parsers (code, csv, JSON)

Immediate mitigations (fast, low-effort):
- For factual-lookup: enforce deterministic numeric formatting post-process (rounding rules) as a stopgap; add targeted unit tests in onboarding harness.
- For multilingual fragility: flag and hold AWQ artifacts for language packs with measured flip-rate > 8% for manual review.
- For code generation: run simple lint-and-parse checks in the onboarding flow; if parse fails, block rollout or fall back to higher-precision artifact.
- For conversational hallucination: increase nucleus sampling threshold tuning for AWQ artifacts during A/B to reduce token-level hallucinations.

Rollout guardrails (proposal):
- Block quantized artifact rollout if any core-business slice exceeds flip-rate 8% and factuality-score delta > 0.06 compared to baseline.
- Require automated parse-check pass rate >= 98% for code/csv/json slices.
- For language-sensitive workloads, require per-language flip-rate < 5% unless customer signs off.

Suggested next experiments (medium term):
- Per-layer calibration probe: run targeted weight re-centering and small retrain of ln/gain on problematic layers for AWQ and re-evaluate flip-rate.
- KV-cache alignment test: reproduce long-context failures with synthetic templates to confirm if token offsets or positional encoding truncation drive errors.
- Mix-precision rollout: evaluate hybrid int8 + int4 where attention remains int8 and FFN quantized to int4; measure flip-rate delta.

Action items (owners):
- Asha P.: Add the 10-slice quick-scan to onboarding checklist and implement flip-rate computation in model-tools (JIRA-AM-4827) — due 2025-03-05.
- Liam O'C.: Add numeric-formatting post-process in eval harness and create unit tests for factual-lookup slice — due 2025-02-28.
- Riley C.: Run per-layer calibration probe (small retrain) for AWQ-int4 on focal problematic model and report back — due 2025-03-12.
- Samira G.: Draft language-specific hold policy and update onboarding docs for multilingual guardrails — due 2025-03-03.

Open questions / risks:
- Are flip-rate thresholds (8%) appropriate across all customers or should we adapt to verticals? (e.g., finance/legal stricter).
- How do we normalize flip-rate across slices of very different base difficulty? (we currently stratify sample difficulty but this needs formalization).
- Long-term: can we build an automated repair step (post-quantize calibration) that reduces flip-rate by >50%  without the cost of full retrain?

Quick reference (TL;DR):
- Use flip-rate as a compact onboarding gate alongside aggregated metric deltas.
- AWQ-int4 shows higher flip-rates on factual and multilingual fragile slices; GPTQ often safer on multilingual but not universally.
- Implement quick mitigations (formatting post-process, parse checks, language holds) and add the 10-slice quick-scan to onboarding.

Appendix (short):
- Raw per-slice numbers and spot-check annotations are pushed to s3://redwood-evals/quant/playbooks/fliprate-v1.tar.gz (see linked_artifacts).
- Quick scripts: model-tools/scripts/compute_fliprate.py (PR linked above).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a lightweight operational note intended for onboarding and release engineers; it is not a comprehensive research audit. Please flag if we should expand the slice set or the spot-check sample sizes before adopting the guardrails.

-- Asha
